https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c62m.text: Image source, Reuters Image caption, President Hakainde Hichilema now wants to build on the foundations that he laid in the first term By Wycliffe Muia Â and Â Damian Zane Published 1 September 2026, 07:43 BST Updated 8 minutes ago Zambia's President Hakainde Hichilema has been sworn in for a second five-year term following a disputed election and the arrest of his main opponent on treason charges. Hichilema - credited with stabilising the economy - swept to victory on 13 August with 60% of the vote, according to official results. Runner-up Brian Mundubile, who received 38%, alleged that the outcome had been tampered with. He was unable to mount a legal challenge to the result as the courts were sealed off last week on the final day a case could be filed. Election observers said that while polling day was largely peaceful, some have raised questions about the vote tallying process. European Union observers said staff in many tallying centres did not record results on tally sheets as soon as they were announced and cited weak verification between digital entries and paper records. It added that returning officers frequently paused proceedings while awaiting instructions from headquarters. The day after the poll, security forces raided a property in the capital, Lusaka, linked to Mundubile, killing a former cabinet minister and arresting a number of opposition politicians. The authorities accused the opposition of planning an armed insurrection, which they denied. Mundubile and his running mate, Makebi Zulu, had gone into hiding. They were detained by police last week and charged at the weekend. When Hichilema, 64, came into office in 2021 after a landslide victory, Zambia had recently defaulted on its international debt and had an annual inflation rate of more than 24%. "We inherited a broken-down countryâ¦ the economy was declining," Hichilema told the BBC in Lusaka before the election. The former businessman negotiated a restructuring of the debt and rebuilt relations with foreign creditors. Inflation has also come down, but prices are still rising and many continue to struggle with the cost of living. Hichilema now wants to build on the foundations he said he laid over the past five years. He was sworn into office on Tuesday amid jubilant scenes, as thousands of supporters gathered to celebrate the inauguration. Presidents from Kenya, Botswana, Zimbabwe, Namibia and Tanzania are among several African leaders attending the inauguration ceremony at the National Heroes Stadium in the capital. Hichilema was sworn in alongside his running mate, Mutale Nalumango. Photograph: Nepal army/EPA Weather tracker Nepal Flash floods destroy villages in central Nepal Landslide blocks river and triggers downstream flooding, while summer temperatures persist in Portugal Matt Andrews and Ed Walton for MetDesk Fri 16 Oct 2026 06.12 EDT First published on Fri 16 Oct 2026 04.51 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Flash floods have swept through Nepal’s central Gorkha district after a pre-dawn landslide on 11 October blocked the Budhi Gandaki River, triggering severe downstream flooding. Two villages in the worst-affected Chumanubri rural municipality were reportedly destroyed, with homes, roads and bridges washed away. Part of a hydropower station was also damaged. After river levels surged from 2 metres to nearly 8.5 metres within hours, the national disaster risk reduction and management authority reported that 204 homes were damaged, and more than 650 people had been affected. More than 100 foreign trekkers were stranded in the popular hiking region. The floods come just two months after catastrophic flooding and landslides devastated parts of the country on the border with Tibet, leaving thousands dead or missing. An exceptionally deep area of low pressure barrelled towards Iceland this week. The central pressure was measured at 931mb on 14 October. The pressure plummeted by 49mb in 24 hours, meeting the thresholds for explosive cyclogenesis, or a weather bomb. The system brought sustained winds of 55–60mph to the southern shores of the island before moving north-east through the North Atlantic towards Norway. However, Iceland was spared the strongest winds as the track of the storm meant they remained out at sea. The system also affected areas beyond Iceland: a 108mph gust was recorded at Bealach Na Bà, in the Scottish Highlands, in association with a trailing 1,000-mile cold front that stretched from Norway to the mid-Atlantic. Summer-like conditions have extended even further into meteorological autumn in Portugal . After temperatures of 40C at the end of September, on 14 October a maximum of 35.6C was recorded in the southern town of Mora, representing a climatological anomaly of more than 10C. The heat was not localised, with numerous stations recording temperatures well into the mid-30s celsius. The latest forecasts show that the high pressure and unseasonably warm upper air temperatures will remain in place for the next few days. Looking further ahead, however, temperatures are expected to slowly return towards the average around the middle of next week.
